exercises.solution: `A` implements only the required `name`, so `A.hello()` uses the default: `Hello, Ana`. `B` overrides `hello`: `Hi Bo!`. Output: `Hello, Ana / Hi Bo!`.

hints: `new` divides by the gcd and makes the denominator positive.
`Display` prints just the numerator when the denominator is 1.
exercises.solution: 2/4 + 1/4 = (2·4 + 1·4)/(4·4) = 12/16 = **3/4**. −3/−9: the sign is moved to make the denominator positive, giving 3/9 = **1/3**. 4/2 is stored as 2/1, and 2 × 1/3 = **2/3**.

hints: String slices compare lexicographically, byte by byte.
In ASCII (and UTF-8), every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase letter.
exercises.solution: `&str` implements `PartialOrd` by comparing bytes in order. "pear" > "apple" because 'p' > 'a', so the first call returns **pear**. 'Z' is byte 90 and 'a' is byte 97, so "Zebra" < "apple" and the second call returns **apple**. For human-friendly ordering you would compare case-folded or locale-aware keys.

exercises.prompt: On a 64-bit machine, how many bytes does a `&dyn Notifier` take?

feedback.message: Not yet. That is the size of a reference to a known type. A trait object reference carries one more pointer.

hints: A trait object reference must find both the data and the right methods for its concrete type.
exercises.solution: A `&dyn Trait` is a **fat pointer**: a pointer to the data plus a pointer to the vtable of the concrete type's methods. Two 8-byte pointers make **16** bytes, as the lesson's program printed.

exercises.prompt: In which situations is `dyn Trait` (dynamic dispatch) a better fit than generics? Choose all that apply.

options.label: A list of plugins loaded from configuration at start-up, each a different type implementing `Plugin`.
options.feedback: Yes. The concrete types are decided at run time and live together in one collection.

options.label: A function that sums any iterator of integers, called in a hot loop.
options.feedback: Not yet. Generics let the compiler specialise and inline the loop; dynamic dispatch would add an indirect call per item.

options.label: A large function instantiated for dozens of types, bloating the binary and slowing builds, where the per-call cost is negligible.
options.feedback: Yes. One copy behind `dyn` can be a sensible trade of a little speed for compile time and binary size.

options.label: Three payment methods that your own crate defines and will not grow.
options.feedback: Not yet. A closed set of variants you own is usually best as an enum, with exhaustive matching and no indirection.

hints: Ask: is the set of types open or closed? Known at compile time or at run time? Is the code hot?
exercises.solution: Use `dyn Trait` for heterogeneous collections whose types are chosen at run time (a) and to avoid monomorphisation bloat when the indirect call doesn't matter (c). Prefer generics for hot, type-specific code (b), and an enum for a closed set of alternatives you own (d).

exercises.prompt: In your own crate, which of these implementations is **not** allowed?

options.label: `impl std::fmt::Display for Fraction` (your type)
options.feedback: Not yet: this is allowed. The type is local to your crate.

options.label: `impl MyTrait for i64` (your trait)
options.feedback: Not yet: this is allowed. The trait is local to your crate.

options.label: `impl std::fmt::Display for Vec<i32>`
options.feedback: Right: both the trait and the type come from the standard library, so the orphan rule forbids it (error E0117).

options.label: `impl From<i64> for Fraction`
options.feedback: Not yet: this is allowed, because `Fraction` is local even though `From` and `i64` are not.

hints: The orphan rule: the trait or the type must be defined in your crate.
exercises.solution: You may implement a trait for a type if at least one of them is local. In (c) both `Display` and the vector type are foreign, so it is rejected with E0117. The usual workaround is a newtype such as `struct Scores(Vec<i32>);`, for which you may implement `Display`.
